overview.summary: Pilots fly aircraft and are responsible for the safe operation of each flight, from planning to landing.
overview.problems: They move passengers and cargo safely between places, often in changing weather and busy airspace.
overview.worksWith: The co-pilot and cabin crew, air traffic controllers, engineers, dispatchers and ground staff.
overview.workplaces: Airline cockpits and airports, and in other roles flight schools, charter companies, cargo operators and helicopter services.

timeline.title: Flight planning and briefing
timeline.description: The pilot checks weather, route, fuel, aircraft status and official notices, then briefs the crew.
timeline.why: Most safety decisions are made before the aircraft moves.

timeline.title: Aircraft checks
timeline.description: The pilot checks the aircraft, sets up the cockpit and works through the checklists.
timeline.why: Checklists catch problems that memory alone can miss.

timeline.title: Take-off and climb
timeline.description: The pilot flies the departure with the co-pilot, follows procedures and talks with air traffic control.
timeline.why: This is a busy phase that needs precision and clear teamwork.

timeline.title: Monitoring and managing the flight
timeline.description: The pilot watches systems, weather, fuel and radio calls and makes adjustments. Much of the cruise phase is monitoring rather than constant manual flying.
timeline.why: Staying alert to small changes prevents bigger problems later.

timeline.title: Approach and landing
timeline.description: The pilot briefs the approach, talks with air traffic control, lands the aircraft and taxis to the gate.
timeline.why: Approach and landing need accuracy and calm decision-making.

timeline.title: Debrief and reporting
timeline.description: The pilot completes reports, notes any aircraft problems and rests within the legal duty limits. Some pilots fly more flights the same day, and others stay overnight away from home.
timeline.why: Reports help engineers fix problems and keep future flights safe.

responsibilities: Planning flights with weather and fuel in mind
Communicating with air traffic control and the crew
Making decisions when something unusual happens
challenges: Schedules are irregular and can include nights, time zone changes and time away from home.
Strict medical checks and regular training and tests are required.
Responsibility for passengers and crew is high.
Training is expensive and the route to a first job can be long.
Managing tiredness is an important part of the job.
Job availability can change with economic conditions.
workEnvironment: The cockpit, airports and hotels used by crews. Flying is mostly done seated, with irregular hours and some nights away from home. Airline, cargo, charter, instructing and helicopter flying differ a lot from one another.
rewards: The satisfaction of operating a complex aircraft safely
A role with clear skills and standards to master
tradeoffs: Time away from family and friends
Disrupted sleep and an irregular routine
A medical or licensing problem can stop you from flying
Pay and conditions vary by airline and country

activity.title: Decode an airport weather report
steps: Open an aviation weather site, such as the Aviation Weather Center at aviationweather.gov, and find the latest weather report, called a METAR, for an airport.
Use a beginner METAR guide to read the wind, visibility, clouds and temperature.
Write one plain sentence describing the weather.
Decide whether the weather looks easy or difficult for flying and explain why.
Note how you felt about studying detailed technical information.
activity.outcome: You practise reading technical information carefully, which pilots do before every flight.
activity.safety: This is for learning only. Never use it to plan or attempt a real flight.

source: Written by Futurixia from general knowledge of how this profession works. It is illustrative and is not based on interviews or surveys.
